summary: Three rescues, each one from something the ancient world considered untouchable. On the far shore Jesus meets a man living among tombs who cannot be restrained, whose demons name themselves Legion and end up drowning a herd of pigs — after which the locals ask him to leave. Back across the lake a synagogue official begs him to come for his dying daughter, and on the way a woman who has bled for twelve years touches his cloak from behind and is healed. Then word arrives that the girl has died, and he goes anyway.
whyItMatters: A corpse, a chronic discharge of blood, and a graveyard were the three great sources of ritual defilement in Jewish law. In this chapter Jesus makes contact with all three, and instead of contamination moving toward him, healing moves outward. That reversal is the chapter's argument.

context.author: Anonymous; early tradition names Mark, recording Peter's preaching
context.audience: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea — Mark translates the Aramaic 'Talitha cumi' and explains nothing about pigs, assuming his readers already keep them
context.setting: The eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee, largely non-Jewish territory, then back to the Jewish western side
context.literaryForm: Narrative, including Mark's signature sandwich — the woman's story is set inside the girl's

keyVerses.text: and saw him who had been possessed by demons sitting, clothed, and in his right mind, even him who had the legion; and they were afraid.
keyVerses.why: The most unsettling reaction in the chapter — the restoration is what frightens them.

keyVerses.text: Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you and how he had mercy on you.
keyVerses.why: The one man in Mark told to go and talk. Notice he is not Jewish — the silence rule does not apply out here.

keyVerses.text: Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be cured of your disease.
keyVerses.why: He stops a life-or-death errand to make sure she is not merely healed but named and sent away in peace. 'Daughter' is the only time he calls anyone that.
Said to a father who has just been told there is no point any more.

questions.question: What does it mean that the demons were called 'Legion'?
questions.answer: A legion was a Roman army unit of several thousand men. The name is the first thing the reader is told about the scale of the problem, and it is not politically neutral in occupied territory — an occupying force that has moved in, cannot be dislodged by force, and destroys the man it inhabits. Mark doesn't press the point. He just uses the word and lets it sit there.

questions.question: Why are there pigs? Weren't pigs forbidden?
questions.answer: To Jews, yes — which is exactly how you know where this scene is happening. The eastern shore was largely Gentile territory, part of the Decapolis, a group of Greek-speaking cities. A herd of two thousand pigs is a normal local industry there and a marker that Jesus has crossed into foreign ground. This is his first extended work among non-Jews.

questions.question: Why destroy someone's livestock? Two thousand pigs is a serious financial loss.
questions.answer: The text does not defend it, and honest readers have found it uncomfortable. What the passage says: the demons asked, and Jesus permitted. Common readings — the drowning gives visible proof that the man is actually free rather than merely calmed; a life is being valued above property; the demons' own destructive nature plays out in the open. It is worth noting Mark reports the herdsmen's reaction without comment, and that the town's response is to ask him to leave. He does not argue with them.

questions.question: Why does the town want him gone after he helped the man?
questions.answer: Mark says plainly that they were afraid, and the sentence structure points at what frightened them: the man sitting there clothed and sane. A wild figure in the tombs was a known quantity you could live alongside. A power that reaches in and changes him is not. There is also the cost — whatever happened here has already destroyed a herd, and nobody knows what it will touch next.

questions.question: Why is this man told to go and tell, when everyone else is told to keep quiet?
questions.answer: It is a real and deliberate reversal, and the geography explains it. In Jewish Galilee, the title 'Messiah' carried the expectation of a warrior king, so publicity was dangerous. In the Decapolis, ten Gentile cities where nobody was waiting for a Jewish deliverer, that risk was absent. So the man becomes the first person in Mark commissioned to talk — and the region he covers is the one Jesus returns to in chapter 7 to find crowds already waiting.

questions.question: Why was the bleeding woman's condition so serious beyond the health of it?
questions.answer: Under Leviticus 15, a discharge of blood made a woman ritually unclean, and anything and anyone she touched became unclean too. Twelve years of that means twelve years of being unable to worship normally and of contact with other people carrying consequences for them. That is why she comes from behind, in a crowd, and touches only his clothes — she is doing something she has been taught is not hers to do, and she is trying not to be seen.

questions.question: 'Who touched my clothes?' — in a crowd pressing on all sides? The disciples think it's a silly question.
questions.answer: They say so, more or less, in verse 31. But Mark distinguishes between the crowd pressing and this one touch, and says Jesus perceived that power had gone out from him. He is not looking for the culprit. Verse 32 says he looked around to see her — and the result is that a woman who had planned to slip away anonymously is instead spoken to, called Daughter, and sent off in peace. She got the healing by stealth. He insists she also get the relationship.

questions.question: Why does Mark interrupt a dying child's story with this?
questions.answer: Because the interruption is the point, and it is his standard technique. The delay is what kills the girl in narrative terms — while Jesus is stopped, the news arrives that she has died. The two stories are also linked by the number twelve: the woman has bled for twelve years, and the girl is twelve years old. One has been dying slowly for as long as the other has been alive. Both are called daughter.

questions.question: Was the girl actually dead, or just asleep as Jesus says?
questions.answer: Readers split here. The mourners had already begun and they laugh at him, so the household considered it settled. Some take 'asleep' literally, as a diagnosis correcting theirs. Most read it the way Jesus uses the word elsewhere — death described as sleep because from where he stands it is not permanent. Mark's own framing supports the second: the messengers say she has died, the professional wailing is under way, and the crowd's reaction to her walking is amazement, not relief at a misdiagnosis.

questions.question: Why does Mark keep the Aramaic words instead of just translating?
questions.answer: 'Talitha cumi' is preserved here, 'Ephphatha' in 7:34, 'Abba' in 14:36, and the cry from the cross in 15:34 — each with a translation attached. Keeping the sound is the mark of a memory passed down by people who heard it. Translating it is the mark of a writer whose readers do not speak that language. Both things are true at once, and together they tell you something about how this book came to be.

questions.question: After raising a girl from the dead, he tells them to keep it quiet and to get her something to eat. Why both?
questions.answer: The silence order is the same pattern as elsewhere in Mark, though here it is close to impossible — a household of mourners is outside. The instruction about food is the detail that gives the scene its texture: she is not a vision or a ghost, she is a hungry twelve-year-old. It is the kind of specific, unnecessary thing that tends to come from someone who was in the room.

glossary.def: A Roman army division of several thousand soldiers. Used here as the demons' self-given name — a statement about number, and an uncomfortable echo in occupied territory.
Literally 'ten cities' — a league of Greek-speaking, largely Gentile cities east and south of the Sea of Galilee.
A ritual status, not a moral or hygienic one. It meant temporarily unfit to approach worship, and it transferred by contact — which is what makes the touching in this chapter significant.
The layman responsible for running the local assembly — arranging services and readings. A respectable community office, which is what makes Jairus falling at Jesus's feet in public notable.
Aramaic, the everyday language Jesus spoke. Mark keeps the sound and supplies the meaning: 'Girl, I tell you, get up.'
